deep.reconstruction:
This page is part of Gauss's table of the decimal periods of fractions with prime denominators. It covers p = 223, 227, 229, 233, 239, 241, 251, 257, 263, 269. The previous page covers 139…211 and the next page 271…317.

For each prime p, let e = ord_p(10) and f = (p-1)/e. The residues mod p split into f cosets of the subgroup <10>. Each coset gives one cycle of digit periods of length e, and Gauss writes one period for each coset.

Convention (my reading, confirmed by the digit counts below): the coloured dots before entries are markers, not digits. The digit string written for the principal cycle is the period of 10/p, i.e. the period of 1/p rotated by one place so that its leading 0 goes to the end. Example: 1/223 = 0.0044843049…; the period written is 0448430493…677130, which is 222 digits.

The small numbers in parentheses or at the ends of rows are cycle labels 0,1,…,f-1. They are evidently indices of the numerators' cosets, presumably with respect to a primitive root (my inference).

The entries:
- p = 223: e = 222, f = 1. One period of 222 digits: 22 groups of 10, then '30'.
- p = 227: e = 113, f = 2. Two periods of 113 digits.
  - Row 1 is the period of 41/227 = 0.1806167400…850220264317. It has 110 + 3 digits; the last digit 7 matches 227N ≡ -41 (mod 10).
  - Row 2 is the period of 10/227: 0440528634…2158590308370.
- p = 229: e = 228. The period of 10/229 has 220 + 8 digits, ending …39301310.
- p = 233: e = 232. The period has 230 + 2 digits, ending …3133047210 30.
- p = 239: e = 7, f = 34, since 10^7 - 1 = 239·41841. Gauss lists all 34 seven-digit periods in five columns.
  - They are labelled (1),(3),…,(33) on alternate entries, read down the columns. The last entry, 0418410 = period of 10/239, is labelled 0.
  - Each entry N satisfies 239·N = k·(10^7 - 1), for example: 4644351 ↔ 111/239, 2552301 ↔ 61/239, 9330543 ↔ 223/239, 6569037 ↔ 157/239, 7489539 ↔ 179/239, 1548117 ↔ 37/239.
  - The label structure is consistent with a cyclic group of cosets. For instance 111^2 ≡ 132 ≡ 61·10 (mod 239), so the coset of index 2 is the square of the coset of index 1.
  - Two entries are struck out and rewritten.
- p = 241: e = 30, f = 8. Eight 30-digit periods in two blocks, labels (2),(4),(6),0. The last one is 0414937759 3360995850 6224066390, the period of 10/241. The first is 5809128630… ≈ 140/241.
- p = 251: e = 50, f = 5. Five 50-digit periods, labels 3 and 0 on rows 3 and 5. The last is the period of 10/251, ending …7968127490. Row 1 ≈ 106/251.
- p = 257: e = 256. The period of 10/257 has 250 + 6 digits, ending …3112840466 926070.
- p = 263: e = 262. The period has 260 + 2 digits, ending …9353612167 30.
- p = 269: e = 268. The period has 260 + 8 digits, ending …38661710.

Purpose: this is the table promised in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 312–318. It converts any fraction with prime denominator to a decimal by locating the numerator's coset via its index, then the starting place within the period.
errors: No arithmetic errors detected in the spot checks: digit counts match ord_p(10) for every prime, and the end digits satisfy p·N ≡ 9 (mod 10) for the 10/p periods.
Two entries at p=239 are struck out (in columns 1 and 2) and replaced; these are corrections Gauss made himself.
Possible missing cycle label at the end of the first row for 227; the row's '317' consists entirely of period digits (113 digits in total).

results.what: Table of decimal periods (all cosets of <10>) for primes 223–269, indexed by cycle/index labels
results.modern_name: Table of periods of decimal fractions / multiplicative order of 10 mod p, coset (index) decomposition of (Z/pZ)^*
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801, arts. 312–318; table published posthumously in Werke II, 1863); also Burckhardt, Reuschle, Goodwyn

results.what: Use of the coset structure: each p with f=(p-1)/ord_p(10) cycles, each labelled by an index, so any r/p can be read off
results.modern_name: Index (discrete logarithm) method for decimal expansion

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working sheet of Gauss's well-known table of decimal periods for denominators under 1000. It is described in the Disquisitiones and printed in Werke II. Nothing non-standard appears.

checkable.asserts: First 227 row is the period of 41/227
Second 227 row is the period of 10/227
Coset of index 2 (61) is the square of the coset of index 1 (111) times 10, consistent with index labelling
The 241 entry labelled 0 is the period of 10/241

transcription_corrections: The dots before entries (e.g. before 0448430493) are coloured markers, not digits.
The trailing '30' at 223, 233 and 263, and '370' at 227 row 2, are final period digits (…3, 0), not separate annotations; at 241 and 251 the final '0' is a cycle label.
